results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The finite grid, exchangeable bounded loss rows, the endpoint condition, and the algorithm applied to their finite tail maxima. For the conditional clause, also an actual regular conditional distribution of the full row matrix given the stated sigma-algebra, with the stated sectionwise assumptions.

[F1] The original rows are exchangeable and their coordinates are measurable and lie in $[0,B]$; the endpoint losses satisfy $L_i(\lambda_M)\le\alpha$ almost surely. [[def-finite-nested-decision-family-and-bounded-risk]]

[F2] The maximum-grid risk-control theorem applies to exchangeable bounded loss rows that are nonincreasing along the finite grid and endpoint-safe. [[thm-finite-grid-conformal-risk-control]]

[F3] Expectation is monotone: if integrable real random variables $X\le Y$ almost surely, then $\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y]$. [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]

[F4] A regular conditional distribution is a probability kernel whose section evaluations satisfy the conditional-event identity for every conditioning event and measurable target set. [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]

[F5] A conditional-expectation version is measurable, integrable, and has the same integrals as the original variable on every event in the conditioning sigma-algebra. [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]

[F6] For nonnegative measurable functions increasing pointwise to a limit, their integrals increase to the integral of the limit. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]



1.1 For each $i$, $\widetilde L_i(\lambda_j)$ is a maximum of finitely many measurable coordinates, so it is measurable and lies in $[0,B]$. The set of indices in the maximum shrinks as $j$ increases, hence $\widetilde L_i(\lambda_{j+1})\le\widetilde L_i(\lambda_j)$. At the endpoint, $\widetilde L_i(\lambda_M)=L_i(\lambda_M)\le\alpha$. The same deterministic row map is applied to every $W_i$, and it commutes with row permutations; therefore the transformed rows remain exchangeable. Each calibration threshold is a finite sum of transformed coordinates, and each first-pass or fallback event is a finite Boolean combination of Borel threshold sets. Thus the selected parameter $\widetilde\lambda(W)$ and the losses $g(W)=L_{n+1}(\widetilde\lambda(W))$ and $h(W)=\widetilde L_{n+1}(\widetilde\lambda(W))$ are Borel functions of the full matrix. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 By [F2], applying the calibration rule to the transformed rows gives $\mathbb E[\widetilde L_{n+1}(\widetilde\lambda)]\le\alpha$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 For every grid index $j$, the maximum defining $\widetilde L_{n+1}(\lambda_j)$ includes $L_{n+1}(\lambda_j)$, so $L_{n+1}(\widetilde\lambda)\le\widetilde L_{n+1}(\widetilde\lambda)$ almost surely. Both variables are bounded and integrable; [F3] and step 1.2 give $\mathbb E[L_{n+1}(\widetilde\lambda)]\le\alpha$. [F3, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 For the conditional clause, let $Q_\omega$ be the stated regular conditional distribution of the full matrix $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_{n+1})$ given $\mathcal T$. For almost every $\omega$, its row law is exchangeable, its coordinates lie in $[0,B]$, and its endpoint losses are at most $\alpha$ almost surely. Applying the same Borel tail-maximum map to each row preserves exchangeability under $Q_\omega$, gives nonincreasing bounded rows, and leaves the endpoint unchanged. The marginal assertion of [F2], applied under each such probability measure $Q_\omega$ to the transformed rows, gives $\int h\,dQ_\omega\le\alpha$. Since $0\le g\le h\le B$ pointwise, [F3] under $Q_\omega$ yields $\int g\,dQ_\omega\le\alpha$. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For each $m\ge1$, put $g_m=2^{-m}\lfloor2^m g\rfloor$. These are finite-valued Borel simple functions increasing pointwise to $g$. Write $g_m=\sum_r c_{m,r}\mathbf 1_{A_{m,r}}$ for Borel level sets $A_{m,r}$ in the full matrix space. By the kernel identity [F4], for every $H\in\mathcal T$, $$\int_H\int g_m\,dQ_\omega\,d\mathbb P(\omega)=\int_H g_m(W)\,d\mathbb P.$$ The kernel integrals of $g_m$ are $\mathcal T$-measurable finite sums of kernel evaluations. By [F6], they increase to $k(\omega)=\int g\,dQ_\omega$, and the right-hand integrals increase to $\int_H g(W)\,d\mathbb P$. Applying [F6] on both sides gives the same identity with $g$ in place of $g_m$. Thus $k$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable, bounded, and has the defining integral identities of a conditional-expectation version by [F5]. Step 2.2 gives $k\le\alpha$ almost surely, proving the conditional bound. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.2, construct] ∎

**Given:** The strictly separable sample, either of the two named losses, arbitrary finite initialization, and the exact fixed-step hypotheses in the Statement. Countable Choice is assumed only for the almost-everywhere clause.

[F1] [[alg-gradient-descent]]: the fixed-step Euclidean update map is $F(w)=w-\eta\nabla\mathcal L(w)$.

[F2] [[def-linear-separable-margin-and-hard-margin-svm]] and [[lem-hard-margin-svm-has-unique-minimizer]]: the bias-free strictly separable finite sample has its unique nonzero hard-margin vector $w^*$.

[F3] [[def-tight-exponential-tail]] and [[lem-logistic-and-exponential-losses-have-tight-exponential-tail]]: both stated loss derivatives satisfy precisely the stated two-sided tight-tail bounds with all six constants one.

[F4] [[lem-recursive-hard-margin-comparison-trajectory]]: the full recursive zero-dual-support construction gives $G_t=\sum_{m=1}^M h_m\log^{\circ m}t+c+o(1)$, $h_1=w^*$, $M\le d$, diverging comparison margins, and defects $\delta_t:=G_{t+1}-G_t+\eta\nabla\mathcal L(G_t)$ satisfying $\sum_t\|\delta_t\|_2<\infty$ for each named loss.

[F5] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis.

[F6] [[lem-nonzero-real-polynomial-zero-set-is-lebesgue-null]]: under Countable Choice, every nonzero finite real polynomial has a Lebesgue-null zero set.

[F7] [[thm-farkas-alternative-for-finite-linear-systems]]: if no nonnegative coefficient vector represents a right-hand side as a linear combination of given columns, a vector pairs nonnegatively with every column and negatively with that right-hand side.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is inherited only by [F6]; it is not used in the all-data argument or in the separate homogeneous Clarke-flow branch.



1.1 Write $v_i=y_ix_i$, $L(w)=\sum_i\ell(v_i^Tw)$, $f=-\ell'>0$ and $F(w)=w-\eta\nabla L(w)$. The sample is nonempty and strictly separable. Choose a unit vector $u$ and $\gamma>0$ with $u^Tv_i\ge\gamma$ for every $i$. For logistic loss, $0<\ell''(s)\le1/4$, so $0\preceq\nabla^2L(w)\preceq\frac14XX^T$. Thus $\beta=\lambda_{\max}(XX^T)/4$ is a global smoothness constant. The stated bound is exactly $\eta<2/\beta$. For exponential loss use the stated $\beta_{\rm loc}$ on the convex region containing the actual update segments, and put $\beta=\beta_{\rm loc}$. Integration of the Hessian along the update segment (or the ordinary Lipschitz-gradient descent inequality) gives $$L(w_{t+1})\le L(w_t)-\eta(1-\eta\beta/2)\|\nabla L(w_t)\|^2.$$ Since $L\ge0$, the gradient squares are summable and $\|\nabla L(w_t)\|\to0$. Meanwhile, $$\|\nabla L(w_t)\|\ge-u^T\nabla L(w_t)=\sum_i f(v_i^Tw_t)u^Tv_i\ge\gamma\sum_i f(v_i^Tw_t).$$ Hence every $f(v_i^Tw_t)\to0$. For both listed losses this forces $v_i^Tw_t\to+\infty$, and therefore $L(w_t)\to0$. In particular $\|w_t\|\to\infty$. No asymptotic directional information has been used in this step. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Here is the elementary comparison fact replacing the full source Lemma 14 case split. For a $C^2$ convex loss $L$, let $x,y$ be such that the Hessian has eigenvalues in $[0,B]$ at every point of the segment $[x,y]$, and suppose $\eta B\le2$. The symmetric matrix $$H_{x,y}=\int_0^1\nabla^2L(y+s(x-y))\,ds$$ has eigenvalues in $[0,B]$, and $\nabla L(x)-\nabla L(y)=H_{x,y}(x-y)$. Therefore $$\|F(x)-F(y)\|=\|(I-\eta H_{x,y})(x-y)\|\le\|x-y\|.$$ For logistic loss this applies globally with $B=\lambda_{\max}(XX^T)/4$ by step 1.1 and the stated step restriction. For exponential loss, no membership of $G_t$ in the assumed local-smoothness region is needed. Let $K=\max_i\|v_i\|^2$. At every $z$, $$\|\nabla^2L_{\exp}(z)\|_{\rm op}\le\sum_i e^{-v_i^Tz}\|v_i\|^2\le K L_{\exp}(z).$$ Convexity gives $L_{\exp}(z)\le\max\{L_{\exp}(w_t),L_{\exp}(G_t)\}$ on the connecting segment $[w_t,G_t]$. Both endpoint losses tend to zero, by step 1.1 and [F4]. Thus on this segment the Hessian bound $B_t=K\max\{L_{\exp}(w_t),L_{\exp}(G_t)\}$ tends to zero. Since $\eta$ is fixed, $\eta B_t\le2$ for every sufficiently large $t$. This proves eventual nonexpansiveness between the actual and comparison iterates, under exactly the stated exponential-loss hypothesis. Choose $T$ large enough for this property and define $r_t=w_t-G_t$. Then $$\|r_{t+1}\|=\|F(w_t)-F(G_t)-\delta_t\|\le\|r_t\|+\|\delta_t\|.$$ Iteration yields $$\sup_{t\ge T}\|r_t\|\le\|r_T\|+\sum_{t\ge T}\|\delta_t\|<\infty.$$ This closes the residual estimate without first assuming any residual growth or sign bound. It is a complete substitute for source Lemmas 14 and 15 in this two-loss theorem. For completeness, the source's scalar recurrence follows directly: for nonnegative $\phi,h,z$ with $\phi_{t+1}^2\le\phi_t^2+h_t\phi_t+z_t$ and $\sum h_t<\infty$, use $h_t\phi_t\le h_t(1+\phi_t^2)/2$ and iterate; $\prod_t(1+h_t/2)\le\exp(\sum h_t/2)$ bounds the product and gives $\phi_{t+1}^2\le C_2+C_3\sum_{s\le t}z_s$, which is precisely the needed Lemma 15 estimate. By [F4], $G_t-\sum_{m=1}^M h_m\log^{\circ m}t$ is bounded. Thus the bounded residual above proves $$w_t=\sum_{m=1}^M h_m\log^{\circ m}t+O(1).$$ In particular $$w_t=w^*\log t+O(\log\log t),\qquad \frac{w_t}{\|w_t\|}\longrightarrow\frac{w^*}{\|w^*\|}.$$ The first convergence uses $h_1=w^*\ne0$ and $\log\log t=o(\log t)$. Any component of the initialization orthogonal to the data span simply remains in the bounded remainder; arbitrary initialization is covered. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Let $I:=\{i:(w^*)^Tv_i=1\}$ be the first-stage active set. It is nonempty: otherwise the finite minimum $\rho:=\min_i (w^*)^Tv_i$ would exceed $1$, and $w^*/\rho$ would be feasible with smaller norm. Let $A$ have columns $v_i$ for $i\in I$. If no $\alpha\ge0$ satisfied $A\alpha=w^*$, [F7] would give $y$ with $v_i^Ty\ge0$ for every $i\in I$ and $(w^*)^Ty<0$. For each inactive $i$, $(w^*)^Tv_i-1>0$; because there are finitely many constraints, choose $\epsilon>0$ small enough that $w^*+\epsilon y$ still satisfies every inactive constraint and that $2\epsilon(w^*)^Ty+\epsilon^2\|y\|_2^2<0$. The active constraints remain satisfied because $v_i^Ty\ge0$. This gives a feasible vector of smaller norm, contradicting minimality. Therefore there is a nonnegative representation $w^*=A\alpha$. [given, F2, F7, step 1.1, construct, algebra, assume-contra, discharge-contradiction]

3.1 Fix the labels. Multiplication $x_i\mapsto v_i=y_ix_i$ preserves Lebesgue-null sets. Outside a finite union of proper polynomial zero sets, every set of at most $d$ of the $v_i$ is linearly independent and no $d+1$ of them lie in one affine hyperplane. The latter excludes the determinant-zero conditions for the augmented rows $(v_i^T,1)$; the former excludes the appropriate Gram determinant-zero conditions. Each relevant polynomial is nonzero, as witnessed by coordinate vectors for the linear conditions and affinely independent points for the affine conditions. By [F6] under [A1], each of these proper polynomial zero sets is Lebesgue null, and so is their finite union. This is the only inherited Countable Choice use. All first-stage active points lie in the hyperplane $(w^*)^Tv=1$, so their number is at most $d$. Their column matrix $A$ has full column rank, and the dual representation is uniquely $$\alpha=(A^TA)^{-1}\mathbf1,$$ because $A^Tw^*=\mathbf1$ and $w^*=A\alpha$. Each coordinate of this rational function has a polynomial numerator not identically zero: for orthonormal columns, every coordinate is $1$. After excluding these finitely many additional numerator-zero sets for every possible active subset, every active multiplier is nonzero. Since the KKT multipliers are nonnegative, they are all positive. Thus every first-stage active index has a simultaneously positive dual representation; [F4] gives $M=1$, and the expansion of step 2.1 gives $w_t=w^*\log t+O(1)$. Restricting this null-set conclusion to the open set of strictly separable arrays proves exactly the almost-everywhere clause in the Statement. This is a consequence, not an extra general-position assumption on the all-data result. [given, F2, F4, F6, A1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The qualification that further logarithms may occur is realized by a concrete separable example. In $\mathbb R^q$ take $n=q$ and $$v_i=e_1+\cdots+e_i\qquad(1\le i\le q).$$ The first hard-margin vector is $e_1$: the first constraint forces $w_1\ge1$ and $e_1$ satisfies all constraints. Its unique dual representation has only the first coefficient positive, because comparison of coordinates from $q$ down to $2$ forces all later coefficients to vanish. After projecting off $e_1$ the same argument applies to the remaining staircase vectors. Consequently $S_m=\{m\}$ and $h_m=e_m$ through $M=q$. Under either stated GD regime the proved expansion is $$w_t=e_1\log t+e_2\log\log t+\cdots+e_q\log^{\circ q}t+O(1).$$ For $q=2$ this gives a nonzero $\log\log t$ residual, and larger $q$ give further nonzero iterated-log coefficients. This also confirms that replacing the all-data proof by only its almost-everywhere branch would lose an actual part of the stated theorem. [given, F2, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Independent $N(0,1)$ exogenous variables and the two recursive Gaussian models in the Example.

[F1] Finite independent sums and affine shifts have the stated characteristic-function formulas. [[def-independent-random-elements]] [[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]]

[F2] The standard normal has density $\phi$, scalar normal laws have characteristic function $\exp(i\mu t-\sigma^2t^2/2)$, and equal scalar characteristic functions determine equal laws. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]] [[thm-uniqueness-of-a-law-from-its-characteristic-function]]

[F3] A finite vector is multivariate normal when every scalar linear projection has its corresponding normal law. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F4] For a nondegenerate Gaussian vector, zero conditional covariance between two coordinates is equivalent to conditional independence given the conditioning coordinates. [[thm-gaussian-zero-partial-correlation-is-conditional-independence]]

[F5] PC deletes a pair at the first conditioning level with a separating set, records that set, orients an unshielded triple as a collider exactly when the middle vertex is absent from its recorded set, then applies R1–R3. [[alg-pc-causal-discovery]]

[F6] The middle vertex of an unshielded triple lies outside a valid separating set exactly when the triple is a collider. [[lem-pc-separating-set-collider]]

[F7] A Gaussian law is faithful to a DAG when its conditional independences agree exactly with that DAG's d-separations. [[def-causal-discovery-oracle-regime]]

[F8] A recursive SCM is Markovian when its exogenous variables are mutually independent; its displayed structural functions define the endogenous variables along the graph. [[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]]

[F9] Under the causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime, population PC terminates and returns the DAG's CPDAG. [[thm-pc-oracle-correctness]]

[F10] D-separation requires every path between the queried vertex sets to be blocked by the conditioning set. [[def-d-separation-in-a-dag]]

[A1] AC is assumed by the supplied Gaussian probability interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]



**Proof technique:** direct covariance calculation and the population PC search.

1.1 Let $W_1,\ldots,W_m$ be a finite independent family of scalar normal variables with means $\mu_r$ and variances $\sigma_r^2$. For any real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_m,b$, [F1]–[F2] give the characteristic function of $b+\sum_r a_rW_r$ as $\exp\!\left(it(b+\sum_r a_r\mu_r)-\frac{t^2}{2}\sum_r a_r^2\sigma_r^2\right)$; scalar uniqueness identifies this as the normal law with that mean and variance. Every scalar projection of a finite affine image of $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_m)$ is such a sum, so [F3] proves that every such image is multivariate normal, including when a projection has variance zero. [F1, F2, F3, A1, construct]

2.1 The chain model's density is $\phi(x)\phi(y-x)\phi(z-y)$, where $\phi$ is the standard-normal density. Its factors are exactly the parent probability kernels $K_X(dx)=N(0,1)(dx)$, $K_Y(x,dy)=N(x,1)(dy)$, and $K_Z(y,dz)=N(y,1)(dz)$, so the full-joint law factorizes in the topological order $X,Y,Z$. All three vertices are observed and [F8] gives the Markovian SCM condition. Its moments are $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=3$, and distinct covariances $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)=2$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)=1$. The vector is multivariate normal by step 1.1, and its covariance matrix is positive definite because $(X,Y,Z)$ is an invertible triangular linear transform of $(U_X,U_Y,U_Z)$. The conditional covariance formula gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z\mid Y)=1-\frac{1\cdot2}{2}=0,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y\mid Z)=1-\frac{1\cdot2}{3}=\frac13,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z\mid X)=2-\frac{1\cdot1}{1}=1.$ Together with the nonzero marginal covariances, [F4] shows that the only conditional independence between distinct variables is $X\perp Z\mid Y$. By [F10], the only d-separated vertex pair is also $X,Z$ given $Y$: the adjacent pairs have an active one-edge path, and the $X$–$Z$ path is blocked only by conditioning on $Y$. Any conditional independence between vertex sets would imply the corresponding coordinate independences, so the set-level independence and d-separation models also agree. This verifies faithfulness in [F7]. [given, F1, F2, F4, F7, F8, F10, A1, algebra]

2.2 The collider model's density is $\phi(x)\phi(z)\phi(y-x-z)$. Its factors are exactly the parent probability kernels $K_X(dx)=N(0,1)(dx)$, $K_Z(dz)=N(0,1)(dz)$, and $K_Y(x,z,dy)=N(x+z,1)(dy)$, so the full-joint law factorizes in the topological order $X,Z,Y$. All vertices are observed and [F8] gives the Markovian SCM condition. Its variances are $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=3$, its covariances are $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)=1$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)=0$. The vector is multivariate normal by step 1.1, and this covariance matrix is positive definite by the invertible triangular map from the exogenous variables. The conditional covariances are $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z\mid Y)=0-\frac{1\cdot1}{3}=-\frac13,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y\mid Z)=1,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z\mid X)=1.$ Therefore [F4] shows that $X\perp Z$ marginally, but there is no conditional independence after conditioning on the third variable and no independence for an adjacent pair. By [F10], this is exactly the collider DAG's d-separation list: the collider path is blocked unconditioned and opened by conditioning on $Y$, while each adjacent pair has an active one-edge path. Any set conditional independence would imply coordinate independences, so [F7] holds at the set level as well. [given, F1, F2, F4, F7, F8, F10, A1, algebra]

3.1 Thus PC does not delete any pair at level $0$. At level $1$, $X-Z$ is deleted and its separator is recorded as $\{Y\}$; $X-Y$ and $Y-Z$ remain because step 2.1 shows that each is dependent both marginally and conditional on the third variable. The sole unshielded triple has its middle vertex in the separator, so [F5] or [F6] leaves both edges undirected. No Meek rule applies without a directed edge, and the output is the undirected chain CPDAG. The run terminates under [F9], since step 2.1 verifies the chain model's discovery-regime hypotheses. [F5, F6, F9, step 2.1, cases]

4.1 PC deletes $X-Z$ at level $0$ and records the empty separator. It retains $X-Y$ and $Y-Z$ by their nonzero marginal covariances. Since $Y$ is absent from the separator, [F5] orients $X\to Y\leftarrow Z$; the output is the collider CPDAG. The run terminates under [F9], since step 2.2 verifies the collider model's discovery-regime hypotheses. These calculations verify both claimed outputs without relying on the diagrams. [F4, F5, F9, step 2.2, cases] ∎

**Given:** Independent Gaussian exogenous variables in the latent model and independent variables $V_X,\varepsilon$ in the direct-edge model.

[F1] A recursive structural causal model may distinguish observed and latent vertices; its Markovian case uses mutually independent exogenous variables. [[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]]

[F2] The causally sufficient discovery regime requires every graph vertex to be observed and the full-joint law to have a parent-kernel factorization, so an omitted latent vertex is outside that regime. [[def-causal-discovery-oracle-regime]]

[F3] Independent scalar normal inputs have product characteristic functions, and finite affine sums use the scalar normal characteristic formula and scalar uniqueness. [[def-independent-random-elements]] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-characteristic-functions-under-affine-maps-and-independent-sums]] [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]] [[thm-uniqueness-of-a-law-from-its-characteristic-function]]

[F4] A finite vector is multivariate normal when every scalar linear projection has its corresponding normal law. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F5] A multivariate normal law has characteristic function $\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)$, and this function uniquely determines its vector law. [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F6] DAGs with the same skeleton and no unshielded colliders are Markov equivalent. [[thm-dag-markov-equivalence-skeleton-vstructures]]

[F7] With two vertices, a CPDAG leaves the only edge undirected when both orientations occur among equivalent DAGs. [[def-cpdag-markov-equivalence-class]]

[F8] PC retains an edge unless a tested conditioning set establishes independence; with two vertices it has no unshielded triples or Meek-rule configurations. [[alg-pc-causal-discovery]]

[F9] Under the causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime, population PC terminates and returns the DAG's CPDAG. [[thm-pc-oracle-correctness]]

[A1] AC is assumed by the Gaussian-law probability interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]



**Proof technique:** covariance comparison and direct inspection of the two-vertex PC search.

1.1 Let $W_1,\ldots,W_m$ be a finite independent family of scalar normal variables with means $\mu_r$ and variances $\sigma_r^2$. For real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_m,b$, [F3] gives the characteristic function of $b+\sum_r a_rW_r$ as $\exp\!\left(it(b+\sum_r a_r\mu_r)-\frac{t^2}{2}\sum_r a_r^2\sigma_r^2\right)$; scalar uniqueness identifies this as the normal law with that mean and variance. Every scalar projection of a finite affine image of $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_m)$ is such a sum, so [F4] proves that every such image is multivariate normal, including when a projection has variance zero. [F3, F4, A1, construct]

2.1 In the latent model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, by independence of $L,U_X,U_Y$. In the direct-edge model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=2$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\tfrac14(2)+\tfrac32=2$. Both vectors are Gaussian by step 1.1 and have the same positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, whose leading principal minors are $2$ and $3$. By [F5], both vector characteristic functions equal $\exp(-t^T\Sigma t/2)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R^2$; the uniqueness clause of [F5] gives equality of the full observed laws. [given, F5, step 1.1, A1, algebra]

3.1 The latent model is a finite recursive Markovian SCM with observed set $\{X,Y\}$ and omitted latent vertex $L$, so it does not satisfy [F2]. The direct-edge model has observed set $\{X,Y\}$ and independent exogenous variables; its full-joint law factors as $N(0,2)(dx)N(x/2,3/2)(dy)$, the root probability kernel for $X$ followed by the probability kernel for $Y$ given its parent $X$. In its two-vertex graph $X\to Y$, the only pair of nonempty disjoint endpoint sets is $\{X\},\{Y\}$, which is not d-separated because of the direct path; step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, so they are not independent. Thus this law is faithful to the direct-edge DAG, and the direct-edge model satisfies the observed-only Markovian factorization and faithfulness conditions in the discovery regime. Since the observed laws agree by step 2.1, no procedure using only that law can distinguish the two causal explanations. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The common observed law has $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1\ne0$, so $X,Y$ are dependent and the perfect oracle does not delete their only edge. With only two vertices there is no unshielded triple and none of R1–R3 applies; by [F9] the regime-compliant run terminates, and its computed output is $X-Y$. Reversing the single edge in the direct-edge DAG keeps the same skeleton and no unshielded collider, so [F6] proves the reverse DAG is equivalent; [F7] therefore gives the same undirected CPDAG. The PC output reports adjacency but cannot recover the latent-versus-direct causal distinction. [F6, F7, F8, F9, step 2.1, step 3.1, A1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The two fixed Borel Bernoulli reward laws, $T=1$, $A_1=2$, and the equiprobable sample space $\Omega=\{0,1\}$ with $Y_1(\omega)=\omega$.

[F1] In the fixed-law finite-arm model, the conditional-mean event identity is stated for every history-and-arm event contained in the chosen-arm event ([[def-adversary-and-feedback-model]]).

[F2] Pseudo-regret is $\sum_t(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t})$, realized reward regret is $\sum_t(\mu^*-Y_t)$, and arm counts sum the indicators of the chosen-arm events ([[def-static-dynamic-and-strongly-adaptive-regret]]).

[F3] For the stated conditional-mean model, the finite-arm lemma gives $\mathbb E[R_T^{\rm rew}]=\mathbb E[\bar R_T]=\sum_i(\mu^*-\mu_i)\mathbb E[N_i(T)]$ ([[lem-finite-arm-regret-decomposes-into-expected-action-counts]]).

[F4] For an event $B$, $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B]=\mathbb P(B)$ ([[cor-expectation-of-an-indicator-is-probability]]).

[F5] Expectation is linear for integrable random variables ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]).
